\section{The decision, the forecast and the testimony}
\label{sec:lttv-forecast}

In March 2015 the CRTC told television distributors to offer, by March 2016, an entry-level service \enquote{priced at no more than \$25 (not including equipment) per month} \citep[para.~26]{crtc2015worldofchoice}. Every discretionary channel was to be available on its own or in small packages by March 2016, and in both forms by December 2016 \citep[para.~47]{crtc2015worldofchoice}. The policy came out of the \textit{Let's Talk TV} proceeding, at which, by one later account, \enquote{virtually all parties expressed concerns about potential impacts of unbundling} \citep[para.~xxii, p.~5]{nordicity2015television}.

In a report dated December 2015, and released by its authors' later account in January 2016 \citep{miller2022rights}, Nordicity and Peter Miller published \textit{Canadian Television 2020}. It was prepared for ACTRA, the Canadian Media Guild, the Directors Guild of Canada, Friends of Canadian Broadcasting and Unifor \citep{nordicity2015television}. It modelled two worlds from 2015 to 2020: a baseline with \enquote{technological and consumer behaviour changes, assuming that the pre-existing broadcasting regulatory regime remains}, and the same world with the CRTC's decisions overlaid \citep[para.~ii, p.~1]{nordicity2015television}. Every headline number is the gap between the two.

By 2020, the report concluded, the decisions were \enquote{likely to result in a loss of \lttvJobsTotal{} FTEs of employment in the Canadian economy}, counted in full-time equivalents, along with \$\lttvGDPTotal{} million of GDP. Of those jobs, \lttvJobsDirect{} were directly in broadcasting and production and \lttvJobsSpinoff{} in other sectors \citep[para.~xliv and Table~1, p.~12]{nordicity2015television}. Those figures sit at the end of a chain. Subscribers move to cheaper unbundled packages; distributors lose retail revenue and pass most of the loss to Canadian channels as lower wholesale fees; weaker channels close; spending on Canadian programming falls; and input-output multipliers turn the spending into jobs and GDP.

The report states the assumptions that drive each link. Subscribers taking the entry-level service with a few chosen channels make up \lttvByopSixteen{} of all subscribers in 2016, \lttvByopSeventeen{} in 2017 and \lttvByopEighteen{} from 2018 \citep[Table~18, p.~76]{nordicity2015television}. Distributors pass \enquote{75\% of their retail revenue loss to Canadian programming services}, having attributed \lttvReportCanShare{} of that loss to Canadian services \citep[paras.~206--207, p.~77]{nordicity2015television}. By 2020, \lttvReportClosuresVI{} of the large integrated companies' Category A and B channels close, and \lttvReportClosuresIndep{} of the independents' \citep[paras.~232--233, p.~85]{nordicity2015television}.

By 2020 the model takes \$\lttvSpecImpactTwenty{} million (\lttvSpecShareTwenty{}) a year out of specialty and pay channels' revenue and \$\lttvBDUImpactTwenty{} million (\lttvBDUShareTwenty{}) out of distributors' revenue, against the baseline \citep[paras.~xxvi--xxvii]{nordicity2015television}.

\subsection{What the committee heard}

On 12 April 2016 Ian Morrison of Friends of Canadian Broadcasting, accompanied by Miller, put the report to the Commons Standing Committee on Canadian Heritage. Its key findings, he said, were that \enquote{by 2020, some 15,130 media jobs will be lost}, along with \enquote{a \$400-million drop in Canadian program expenditures} that was \enquote{18\% of what now exists}, \enquote{all of this as the direct result of Let's Talk TV regulatory changes} \citep[time marks 0900--0905]{commons2016chpc8}.

Each phrase is stronger than the report. The \lttvJobsTotal{} FTEs are economy-wide, and \lttvJobsSpinoff{} of them are spin-off employment in other sectors; the \lttvCPEShareStated{} is a share of the report's projected 2020 baseline, not of current spending; and the report itself splits its total into direct and spin-off impact. The figure also fails to reproduce. The report's own baseline-scenario figures put 2020 Canadian programming expenditure at \$\lttvCPEBaselineTwenty{} million, so its \$\lttvCPEImpactTwenty{} million reduction is \lttvCPEShareTwenty{} of baseline, not the \lttvCPEShareStated{} its text states \citep[para.~239; Figs.~8, 9, 43]{nordicity2015television}. Against what existed when Morrison spoke, the report's own figure for 2015 spending, the reduction is \lttvCPEShareFifteen{}. None of the \lttvCPENCandidates{} shares I could build from the report's figures, over \lttvCPENDenominators{} denominators and its two impact figures, gives \lttvCPEShareStated{} (table~\ref{tab:cpe-denominators}).

Morrison also offered a forecast of his own, one month after the entry-level service launched: \enquote{the best estimates I've seen, Mr.~Waugh, are that about 4\% of Canadians will go for it} \citep[time marks 0920--0925]{commons2016chpc8}.

\section{How the forecast was checked}
\label{sec:lttv-method}

The prediction record (forecasters, quantities, paths by year, stated assumptions) was committed before any outcome series was downloaded. I then re-read the report's two paths from the data labels on its charts, checking every value against the totals in its text, and ran a design analysis by fake-data simulation before opening any CRTC file \citep{gelman2014types, gelman2020workflow}. It asked, for each forecast quantity, whether the outcome could separate a world in which the report's impact occurred from one in which it didn't, given that the baseline itself could be wrong.

That last clause is the hard part. In retrospective analysis of regulation, \enquote{developing a credible counterfactual is the most demanding aspect}, and the baselines assumed beforehand \enquote{must be revisited} to see whether outside factors changed the result \citep[286]{morgenstern2018retrospective}. Here the counterfactual is the report's own no-reform baseline, itself a forecast of how television would have fared under streaming without the reforms. So the check treats the baseline's error as unknown, puts a range on it, and reports results across that range, much as \textcite{kane2026sffa} reports against more than one baseline.

It depended on the quantity. With the baseline's error set at the volatility of the report's own 2010--2014 data, specialty and pay revenue would be classified correctly in about \lttvDesignCorrectSpec{} of simulated worlds and distributors' revenue in about \lttvDesignCorrectBDU{}. Canadian programming expenditure, whose historical volatility was \lttvHistSDCPE{} a year, came out at \lttvDesignCorrectCPE{}, so it was set aside in advance as descriptive.

The outcome measure is a single number, \(k\): the observed shortfall below the report's baseline over 2016--2019, the four years before the pandemic, as a multiple of the report's own forecast impact, so that \(k=0\) is no effect and \(k=1\) is the forecast. In logs, \(\log B_t-\log Y_t=k\,\delta_t+e_t\), where \(B_t\) is the report's baseline, \(Y_t\) the outcome, \(\delta_t\) the report's forecast shortfall, and \(e_t\) the baseline's error (positive when the baseline overstates what would have happened without the decisions), modelled as a random walk from 2014. The report's paths and the CRTC series are both in nominal dollars, and since \(k\) compares them year by year, deflating both by the same price index leaves it unchanged.

The 95\% interval for \(k\) comes from generalized least squares under that model, and it reflects only the assumed error in the baseline, so its width depends on how large that error is taken to be. The scale of that error is calibrated from an outside comparison, described below, rather than estimated from four years of outcomes, and the CRTC's administrative totals are treated as measured without error (appendix~\ref{app:methods}; inputs in table~\ref{tab:inputs}).

\(k\) compares the outcome with the report's two forecast paths; it isn't an estimate of the decisions' causal effect, which would need a better counterfactual than the report's own baseline. The forecasters' own cited inputs (uptake between \lttvCitedUptakeLow{} and \lttvCitedUptakeHigh{}, closures up to \lttvCitedClosuresMult{} times the assumed rate) define a band of \(k\) that counts as consistent with their forecast. An outcome below the forecast path was to be reported as the forecast exceeded, never as confirmed.

How wrong the baseline was can't be known from the outcomes, so the plan fixed an external check: the report's forecast of US Netflix subscribers, which Canadian regulation couldn't affect, against Netflix's reported US paid memberships \citep{netflix2019form10k}. The report forecast \lttvNetflixFcEighteen{} million for 2018 and Netflix reported \lttvNetflixObsEighteen{} million, which by the pre-stated rule puts the error at \lttvSigmaTech{} a year, below the historical volatility of both revenue series. The CRTC series reproduce the report's 2012--2014 values within \lttvSpliceTol{} \citep{crtc2017sfs2016, crtc2021sfs2020}.

\section{What happened}
\label{sec:lttv-results}

Figure~\ref{fig:paths} shows each revenue series against the report's two paths. Specialty and pay revenue stayed above the report's no-reform baseline, by between \lttvSpecVsBaselineMin{} and \lttvSpecVsBaselineMax{} from 2016 to 2019, and ran between \lttvSpecVsLTTVMin{} and \lttvSpecVsLTTVMax{} \lttvSpecAboveLTTV{} the forecast path. Taken alone, the revenue \lttvSpecRevNomDir{} \lttvSpecRevNomChange{} in nominal dollars from 2015 to 2019 and \lttvSpecRevRealChange{} after inflation, while the report's baseline was flat in nominal dollars over 2016--2019 (table~\ref{tab:inputs}).

\begin{figure}[tbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/lttv_paths.pdf}
\caption{Revenue relative to the report's no-reform baseline, 2012--2019, in per cent of the baseline. The forecast path and the baseline are the report's (Figs.~41, 42); the model at counted uptake is the report's chain with uptake held at the CRTC's June 2016 count (post hoc); the outcome is the CRTC series (2016 release to 2015, 2020 release after; channels exclude exempt services). The shaded range is the 95\% range of the no-reform outcome under the baseline-error model at the pre-stated \(\sigma\) (\lttvSigmaReadSpec{} and \lttvSigmaReadBDU{} a year). Before 2015 the baseline is the report's own actual values. Both panels share one scale.}
\label{fig:paths}
\end{figure}

At the pre-stated calibration \(\hat k=\lttvKSpec\), with a standard error of \lttvKSpecSE{}. That's \lttvKSpecSEsFromZero{} standard errors from no effect and \lttvKSpecSEsFromOne{} from the forecast, and the lowest value the forecasters' own inputs imply, \lttvBandSpecLo{}, is \lttvKSpecSEsFromBandLo{} standard errors away. The pre-stated reading follows: the 95\% interval, \lttvKSpecLoTwo{} to \lttvKSpecHiTwo{}, lies below the band of \lttvBandSpecLo{} to \lttvBandSpecHi{}, so the outcome is inconsistent with the forecast at the report's assumed uptake.

That band assumes uptake of the entry-level package between \lttvCitedUptakeLow{} and \lttvCitedUptakeHigh{}, and uptake was far lower (section~\ref{sec:lttv-links}). Model-implied scenarios show how much of the gap the failed input accounts for (table~\ref{tab:scenarios}). With uptake held at the CRTC's count for June 2016, \lttvUptakeJuneShare{}, and every other input as the report had it, the report's chain gives \(k=\lttvKPredSpecObsUptake\), \lttvKPredSpecObsUptakeSEs{} standard errors from the estimate. Held at Morrison's estimate of \lttvMorrisonUptake{} it gives \lttvKPredSpecMorrison{} (\lttvKPredSpecMorrisonSEs{} standard errors away), and at the low end of the cited range \lttvKPredSpecCitedLow{} (\lttvKPredSpecCitedLowSEs{}). Since later uptake is unknown, two rising paths start from the 2016 count: rising to \lttvMorrisonUptake{} by 2019 gives \lttvKPredSpecRiseMorrison{} (\lttvKPredSpecRiseMorrisonSEs{}), and rising to \lttvCitedUptakeLow{} gives \lttvKPredSpecRiseCitedLow{} (\lttvKPredSpecRiseCitedLowSEs{}).

The scenarios don't fall to zero because the forecast's channel losses from faster cord-cutting and from closures don't depend on uptake. At counted uptake the outcome is consistent with the scenario, which doesn't confirm the model. None of these scenarios was in the analysis plan; they were added after an outside reader asked how a failed assumption can be told from a failed mechanism, and they sit beside the pre-stated reading rather than replacing it (table~\ref{tab:chronology}).

Distributors' revenue ran between \lttvBDUVsLTTVMin{} and \lttvBDUVsLTTVMax{} \lttvBDUAboveLTTV{} the report's forecast path, falling from \$\lttvBDURevFifteen{} million in 2015 to \$\lttvBDURevNineteen{} million in 2019, a fall of \lttvBDURevNomChange{}, or \lttvBDURevRealChange{} after inflation. Here \(\hat k=\lttvKBDU\) (standard error \lttvKBDUSE{}), \lttvKBDUSEsFromZero{} standard errors from no effect and \lttvKBDUSEsFromOne{} from the forecast, so the outcome is consistent with the forecast and with the band of \lttvBandBDULo{} to \lttvBandBDUHi{} implied by the forecasters' inputs (interval \lttvKBDULoTwo{} to \lttvKBDUHiTwo{}). At the uptake the CRTC counted, though, the report's chain gives only \(k=\lttvKPredBDUObsUptake\), \lttvKPredBDUObsUptakeSEs{} standard errors below the estimate, which suggests that some of the distributors' loss came from outside the model's unbundling channel.

\begin{figure}[tbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/lttv_k_sigma.pdf}
\caption{The estimate of \(k\) and its 95\% interval as a function of the assumed annual error in the report's baseline, \(\sigma\). The solid vertical line marks the pre-stated calibration; dotted lines mark the values of \(\sigma\) used by the other calibrations (table~\ref{tab:calibrations}). The grey band is the range of \(k\) implied by the forecasters' cited inputs. The standard error is proportional to \(\sigma\), so the interval widens linearly while the estimate stays put.}
\label{fig:k-sigma}
\end{figure}

Both intervals depend on how wrong the baseline is taken to be (figure~\ref{fig:k-sigma}). The estimates don't move as the assumed error grows; the intervals widen in proportion. The specialty and pay interval reaches the band implied by the forecasters' inputs once the error exceeds \lttvCutoffSpec{} a year, and at the widest calibration, \lttvSigmaWidest{}, its upper end is \lttvKSpecHiWidest{}. The distributors' interval includes zero once the error exceeds \lttvCutoffBDU{}. No interval for specialty and pay revenue excludes zero at any calibration, which isn't evidence that the effect was zero \citep{gelman2014statcrisis, gelmanStern2006difference}.

The pre-stated Netflix comparison puts the error at \lttvSigmaTech{} a year, below both series' historical volatility, so the historical volatility sets the pre-stated interval. Other defensible readings of the comparison give more: the 2016 miss gives \lttvSigmaTechSixteen{} a year and a pooled estimate \lttvSigmaTechPooled{}. Part of the 2016 miss is an inherited offset, since the report's 2015 starting figure (\lttvNetflixFcFifteen{} million) was already above Netflix's count (\lttvNetflixObsFifteen{} million) \citep{netflix2018form10k}. Measured as growth, Netflix outran the forecast, by \lttvNetflixObsGrowth{} against \lttvNetflixFcGrowth{} from 2015 to 2018, which puts the error at \lttvSigmaGrowthEighteen{} a year.

A check of the model, added after the outcome data was opened, finds the specialty and pay residual concentrated in its first step. Under the model the standardized yearly errors of the baseline should look like independent standard normal draws. For specialty and pay revenue the step from 2014 to 2016 is \lttvInnovSpecFirst{}, and none of the three later steps exceeds \lttvInnovSpecLaterMax{} in absolute value; the distributors' steps show no such pattern. A one-time gap between the report's baseline and the CRTC series would produce this, though with four points so would a random walk whose later steps happened to be small.

In 2015, a year with no forecast impact, the report's own figure (itself a forecast) already shows the gap. The CRTC later counted \$\lttvCRTCFifteenSpec{} million of specialty and pay revenue, \lttvGapFifteenSpec{} \lttvGapFifteenSpecDir{} the report's \$\lttvReportFifteenSpec{} million; for distributors the count was \lttvGapFifteenBDU{} \lttvGapFifteenBDUDir{} the report's figure. The CRTC's 2016 and 2020 releases agree on 2016 to within \lttvReleaseGapMax{}, so the change of release isn't the source. Allowing a level offset in the model gives \(\hat k=\lttvKSpecOffset\) (standard error \lttvKSpecOffsetSE{}) for specialty and pay revenue and \lttvKBDUOffset{} (\lttvKBDUOffsetSE{}) for distributors' revenue, leaving both readings as they were.

\section{The links in the chain}
\label{sec:lttv-links}

The report's own inputs can be checked without a counterfactual, and they show where its chain parted from events. The decisive one is uptake. The report took its \lttvByopEighteen{} from outside estimates, the highest being Oliver Wyman's finding that \enquote{as many as 35\% of subscribers would be willing to switch} \citep[para.~201, p.~75]{nordicity2015television}. The CRTC counted \lttvUptakeAprilN{} subscribers to the entry-level package five weeks after launch \citep{crtc2016basicpackage} and \lttvUptakeJuneN{} by 30 June 2016 \citep[para.~12]{crtc2016hearing0907}, \lttvUptakeAprilShare{} and \lttvUptakeJuneShare{} of all subscribers, against the report's \lttvByopSixteen{} for 2016. I found no later count. Low uptake may partly reflect how the package was sold. The CRTC's hearing of September 2016 examined \enquote{the practices certain providers have adopted in offering} it \citep[para.~5]{crtc2016hearing0907}. Either way, the condition on which most of the forecast rested didn't hold.

The report also assumed a path for what distributors pay Canadian channels. In its no-reform baseline the monthly fee per subscriber for Canadian specialty and pay services rises \lttvBaseFeeGrowth{} from 2015 to 2019 \citep[Table~14, p.~67]{nordicity2015television}, and under the decisions it falls below that path as distributors pass on \lttvReportPassThrough{} of their losses. What distributors paid Canadian channels rose from \$\lttvPayCanFifteen{} million in 2015 to \$\lttvPayCanNineteen{} million in 2019 while subscribers fell, so per subscriber it rose \lttvPerSubGrowth{}, and the Canadian share of all affiliation payments stayed near \lttvPayShareFifteen{} \citep[Table~U-T11]{crtc2019cmrbdu}. After inflation the total \lttvPayCanRealDir{} \lttvPayCanRealChange{} and the payment per subscriber \lttvPerSubRealDir{} \lttvPerSubRealChange{}; the comparison with the report's fee path needs no such adjustment, since that path is nominal too. With so little uptake there was little loss to pass on, so this mainly shows that the baseline fee path was too pessimistic; still, fees ended above the report's no-reform path, where the decisions scenario puts them below it.

The aggregates don't show why fees rose. Some of the payments stay inside the integrated groups, and the report itself expected those groups' revenue impact to be partly offset \citep[para.~227, p.~83]{nordicity2015television}. The CRTC's wholesale code, in force from January 2016 \citep[p.~73, n.~82]{nordicity2015television}, is in both of the report's scenarios \citep[p.~72, n.~80]{nordicity2015television}, so its fee path already allows for it.

Closures are the one input that came out close to the report. Between \lttvClosVILo{} and \lttvClosVIHi{} of the integrated companies' Category A and B channels stopped operating by 2019--2020, against the report's \lttvReportClosuresVI. For the independents the bounds run from \lttvClosIndLo{} to \lttvClosIndHi{}, because channels that left licensing for exemption can't be told apart from channels that closed. Canadian programming expenditure, read only descriptively, stayed at or above the baseline path through 2019.

The last link, from revenue to jobs, can be checked for two of the sectors, because the CRTC's summaries report staff counts \citep{crtc2017sfs2016, crtc2021sfs2020}. The report gives its direct FTE losses by sector against a baseline whose employment path it doesn't publish, so the comparison is with the change from 2015 and with the 2012--2015 trend carried forward, a crude stand-in for that baseline. Channels' staff fell from \lttvStaffChanFifteen{} in 2015 to \lttvStaffChanNineteen{} in 2019, \lttvStaffChanVsTrend{} \lttvStaffChanVsTrendDir{} the trend, against a forecast direct loss of \lttvStaffChanForecast{} by 2019. Distributors' staff stayed near its pre-2015 trend, \lttvStaffDistVsTrendEighteen{} \lttvStaffDistVsTrendEighteenDir{} it in 2018 and \lttvStaffDistVsTrend{} \lttvStaffDistVsTrendDir{} it in 2019, against a forecast direct loss of \lttvStaffDistForecast{} by 2019 \citep[Table~22, p.~91]{nordicity2015television}. The 2019 figure is a one-year jump that reverses the next year, which may be a reporting discontinuity.

Observed staffing doesn't track the revenue chain in either sector: channels cut staff while their revenue held, and distributors' staffing stayed near trend while their revenue fell (annual series in table~\ref{tab:staff}). It's a descriptive mismatch, not a test of the model's employment prediction. The counts aren't the report's modelled full-time equivalents, the distributor series changes from an FTE count to a staff count between releases (the two differ by \lttvStaffDistVintageGap{} in 2016), and a straight-line trend is a weak counterfactual. The direction of the mismatch holds with the distributors' 2018 figure in place of 2019.
